name: Vera Molnar
bio: Vera Molnar (1924–2023) was one of the first artists to make work with a computer. Trained in Budapest, she moved to Paris in 1947 and was a co-founder of the Groupe de Recherche d'Art Visuel in 1960. Before she had access to a machine she worked with what she called a 'machine imaginaire': she wrote simple rules and executed them by hand, systematically varying squares, lines and grids. In 1968 she began working on a computer at a university research centre in Paris, writing programs in Fortran and Basic and drawing the results with a plotter. Series such as Interruptions (1968–69), (Des)Ordres (1974) and Lettres de ma mère (1981–90) explore how a small dose of randomness, '1% disorder', brings an ordered system to life. She worked until her death in 2023, a few months before her centenary; the Centre Pompidou opened a major exhibition of her work in 2024.
studyNotes: Rules first, machine second. Her 'machine imaginaire' shows that algorithmic thinking does not need a computer; write the rule, then run it by hand.
One per cent disorder. Introduce a small amount of randomness into a strict system and watch where it breaks; that tension is the work.
Series, not single images. She explored a rule across hundreds of variations; the meaning is in comparing them.
Sixty years of the same questions. From the 1950s to the 2020s she kept working with squares and lines; the depth comes from long, patient iteration.
